↳ Posted by fidicen on November 10th, 2002.

A lot of dance tunes and marches in the Great Highland Bagpipe repertoire have four parts (some of the 3rd and 4th parts are probably later additions to older 2-part tunes). Many of these tunes have filtered through into the Irish tradition, either berfore they acquired their additional pars, or losing them in the process. on the other hand, some tunes, such as Lord MacDonald’s and The Mason’s Apron, started off in Scotland as 2-part tunes, and gained more parts in Ireland.

↳ Posted by Kenn on November 11th, 2002.

Over the centuries there has been so much cultural coming and going between Ireland and other parts of the British Isles (and America, and Canada, and …) that the grey area between music that is of genuine Irish origin and music that isn’t must be getting larger by the minute, and is irreversible. And now I discover that Jenny Goes To Linton aka The High Road To Linton is Scottish! I don’t see how we can draw a clear line of demarcation, and in a large number of cases it is probably impossible to identify the origin of a tune.
Basically I’m inclined to accept anything that is celtic in origin - which I suppose would in theory exclude morris dances and other English country tunes. But then some of those must have migrated to Ireland at some stage and became accepted. And what about some French tunes which may have been brought back to Ireland by soldiers returning from the Napoleonic Wars? A lot of the donegal music is distinctly Scottish in feel - I’ve posted some recently. And then there’s all that wonderful stuff coming from Shetland. I could go on, but you get the picture. I don’t think it’s possible to keep this site a strictly Irish site, although most people I’m sure try to keep it predominantly Irish.
I’m not sure whether ABC can cope with the non-diatonic notes in Scottish bagpipe tuning though.
Now that “Brollum” tune looks interesting …
-m

High Road to Linton 4 parts

Info on the title

I was interested to read in the Fiddler’s Companion that the title is thought to refer to the old drove road through West Linton in the NW Scottish Borders, nicknamed the “Thieves’ Road”. Oranaiche

“With most Scottish tunes (piobearachd, as they’re called) they originated as a ONE part tune, and many have been evolved into 4 and 6 part tunes, with the other 3 or 5 parts being variations on the first, original part… not true with ALL, but by any means true for many.”

You are on the right track here but Piobaireachd is a genre and tunes are not called Piobaireachd unless they are one…they are the classical music of the pipes dating back to the 16th Century…They have a theme or ground and build in melodic variations and return to the ground at the end. This can be called Ceol mor or “great” or “big” music but everything else (Jigs/Hornpipes/Marches/Strathspeys/Reels) can be called Ceol beag or “little” or “lite” music…..

↳ Posted by Filosmusic on June 16th, 2019.

Re: The High Road To Linton

Many years ago I was told by a stalwart of the revival who was in a position to know that the standard C and D parts are by Sean McGuire. I won’t name the source in case I’ve misremembered what he said, but it does sound like it could well be McGuire’s handiwork, even though I can’t find any concrete evidence.

fidicen mentioned the connections between the different traditions on these isles, and that Shetland music should be welcome on this site. What isn’t commonly known is that Irish music had an influence there, because for many years they had better reception of Irish radio than of Scottish stations.

And I know a couple of serious scholars of English music who argue that the forms and ornamentation and many of the older tunes of the Irish tradition owe much more to English fiddling that is commonly recognised. I think for many in Scotland and Ireland the English tradition is underestimated.

And as for the Scottish and Irish traditions, they are deeply interwoven, as this tune illustrates. My gut feel is that it’s Scottish, but we’ll never really know.

Once you understand these complex interconnections, narrow parochialism begins to look rather foolish. So let’s celebrate the rich diversity, while also respecting our common roots.

Can anyone shed some light on whether the Amix versus Amajor versions are regional (or Irish versus Scottish) variants or something else? Or maybe it turned into A major more recently? Or something to do with fact that on some pipes the G natural is slightly sharp?

In the Robin Williamson book “English, Welsh, Scottish, & Irish Fiddle Tunes” it’s in Amix (written with 3 sharps but all the Gs have a natural sign). That book’s from the 70s. The tune’s in the Scottish section.

Hanneke Cassel says she learned it on the Isle of Skye and plays it in A major:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQQVXMwq0j0

And Alasdair Fraser plays it in A major:
https://alasdairfraser.bandcamp.com/track/the-sweetness-of-mary-devil-in-the-kitchen-willie-davie-the-sound-of-mull-the-high-road-to-linton

Though it’s possible that Fraser is doing an ambiguous G natural/sharp. I didn’t run it through the slow downer to check too hard.

↳ Posted by Calum on December 3rd, 2022.

Re: The High Road To Linton

In my experience of this tune (in Scotland) I’ve only ever heard a G natural in the second part and usually a G# in the fourth part unless there are small pipes present - I don’t normally hear any G notes in the first and third parts.

I tend to accompany this as if in A major but avoid playing any G notes.
For the second part I often play something like:
|:A D5|A/C# Bm7|A/C# D5| E7no3:|
using the shapes:
A = x0543x, Bm7 = 7x77xx, A/C# = 9x79xx, D5 = x577xx, E7no3 = 07x7xx
